hint: Git has no opinion about it.

choices.text: A setting inside Git that decides how merges work
choices.why: There is no workflow setting; Git merges whatever it is asked to.

choices.text: The order of commands in a lesson
choices.why: It is about branches and merging, for a whole team.

choices.text: A plugin installed on GitHub
choices.why: No tool is needed; it is an agreement.

choices.text: A team's agreement about how branches are used
choices.why: Right. Git will do whatever the agreement says.

prompt: A feature branch has lived for three weeks while main received twenty merges. What is the likely cost?

choices.text: Git will refuse to merge a branch that old
choices.why: Git has no age limit. It merges, with whatever conflicts result.

choices.text: A large merge, with many conflicts at once
choices.why: Right. The more both sides changed, the more lines they share.

choices.text: The branch's commits will be lost
choices.why: Nothing is lost; the cost is the reconciliation.

choices.text: None, if the branch has a clear name
choices.why: The name does nothing about drift.

prompt: Which habits keep feature branches healthy? Choose all that apply.
hint: Both are about size and drift.

choices.text: Bringing main into the branch every day or so
choices.why: Yes. Conflicts then arrive one at a time.

choices.text: Splitting the work so each branch is small
choices.why: Yes. Small branches merge and review easily.

choices.text: Keeping the branch private until it is finished
choices.why: Hiding it longer makes the final merge bigger.

choices.text: Making one big pull request at the end
choices.why: Big pull requests get approved, not read.

prompt: What does trunk-based development ask of each developer?
hint: Trunk is an old name for main.

choices.text: To keep one branch per feature until it is released
choices.why: That is closer to Git Flow.

choices.text: To never use branches at all
choices.why: Short branches are common in trunk-based teams.

choices.text: To merge only on release days
choices.why: The opposite: merging is daily, releasing may be too.

choices.text: To integrate into main at least once a day
choices.why: Right. Directly, or through a branch that lives hours.

prompt: sunday_hours = off is in main and in production. What does that mean?
hint: Merged is not the same as switched on.

choices.text: Merged, and nobody sees it yet
choices.why: Right. Changing off to on shows it, with no merge.

choices.text: The Sunday hours code was deleted
choices.why: It is there, switched off.

choices.text: The feature is waiting on its own branch
choices.why: It is in main already; that is the point of the flag.

choices.text: The deploy failed, and a setting records it
choices.why: A flag is deliberate, not a record of failure.

prompt: The Sunday hours feature is switched on and something goes wrong. Why is switching it off faster than a revert?

choices.text: A revert cannot undo a feature
choices.why: It can; it is just slower and touches more.

choices.text: It needs no commit, review or deploy
choices.why: Right. One setting changes and the old behaviour returns.

choices.text: Flags are stored in Git's reflog
choices.why: Flags are the program's settings, nothing to do with the reflog.

choices.text: Reverts are forbidden on main
choices.why: Reverts are the normal undo on main, lesson 4.

prompt: What does trunk-based development need in order to work? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them is Git Flow's, not trunk's.

choices.text: Checks that catch a mistake within minutes
choices.why: Yes. main changes too often for mistakes to wait.

choices.text: Flags removed once a feature is fully on
choices.why: Yes. Otherwise switches pile up.

choices.text: A separate develop branch for unfinished work
choices.why: That is Git Flow. Trunk keeps unfinished work in main, switched off.

choices.text: The skill of splitting work into small changes
choices.why: Yes. Daily integration needs daily-sized pieces.

prompt: Match each Git Flow branch to what it holds.
hint: One description on the right is trunk based, not Git Flow.

pairs.right: Released versions only, each one tagged
Finished work collecting for the next release
A version being prepared: only fixes go in
An urgent fix to a released version

right_distractors: Unfinished work switched off by a flag

prompt: In Git Flow, why does a hotfix merge into both main and develop?
hint: Where would the fix be missing otherwise?

choices.text: Because Git requires two merges for a tag
choices.why: Tags need no merges at all.

choices.text: To create a backup of the fix
choices.why: Every clone is a backup; the second merge is about the next release.

choices.text: Because hotfix branches cannot be deleted
choices.why: They are deleted once merged, as in the capture.

choices.text: So the next release has the fix too
choices.why: Right. Without the second merge, 1.2 would bring the bug back.

prompt: Which product is Git Flow the best fit for?
hint: Are there real versions, with old ones still supported?

choices.text: A web shop deployed twenty times a day
choices.why: There is no version 1.1 in any meaningful sense; Git Flow is ceremony there.

choices.text: A mobile app released as versions after a store review
choices.why: Right. Versions are real, and a fix to one must not wait for the next.

choices.text: A two-person bakery site
choices.why: Far too heavy: six merges for two features.

choices.text: An internal report updated every morning
choices.why: Nothing there is versioned or supported in parallel.

prompt: In the capture, Git Flow needed ___ merge commits for two features, one release and one fix.
Which question decides the workflow, according to this lesson?
hint: It is about the people using the software.

choices.text: How many developers are on the team?
choices.why: Size matters less than how software is shipped.

choices.text: How fast does main reach its users?
choices.why: Right. The answer points at one of the three shapes.

choices.text: Which hosting service does the team use?
choices.why: All three shapes work on every service.

choices.text: How long is the average commit message?
choices.why: Messages matter, lesson 11, but they do not choose a workflow.

prompt: A new team with no strong reason either way: which shape does the lesson recommend starting with?
hint: The one hosting services are built around.

choices.text: Git Flow, to be ready for versions
choices.why: Ceremony they may never need.

choices.text: Trunk based, since it is the most advanced
choices.why: It needs checks and habits a new team may not have yet.

choices.text: Short feature branches
choices.why: Right. Review from the first day, and a short step to trunk based.

choices.text: No branches, everybody on main
choices.why: That skips review entirely.

prompt: A short file in the repository that writes the workflow down is usually called ___.md
hint: It tells people how to contribute.

prompt: Match each team to the workflow that fits it.
hint: Ask how its software reaches users.

pairs.left: Deploys main automatically many times a day, with strong checks
Ships numbered versions and still fixes the previous one
Releases when somebody decides, a few times a week

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of them is about Git itself having an opinion.

choices.text: Git enforces the workflow a team chooses
choices.why: Git has no opinion; the hosting service's rules and the team's habits do the enforcing.

choices.text: A short feature branch merges with fewer conflicts than a long one
choices.why: Yes. Less time for both sides to touch the same lines.

choices.text: A feature flag lets unfinished work be merged safely
choices.why: Yes. Merged, not switched on.

choices.text: Git Flow's main holds only released versions
choices.why: Yes, each one tagged.

choices.text: Trunk based means never reviewing code
choices.why: Reviews happen, on small changes, the same day.
